Learning to delegate was the hardest part of becoming a tech lead.
I delegate the washing-up to the kids.

synonyms.note: Give a task formally, often from a list.
Give responsibility to someone you trust.

otherMeanings.meaning: (noun, /ˈdelɪɡət/) A person sent to represent others, for example at a conference.
otherMeanings.example: Over three hundred delegates attended the conference in Manchester.
otherMeanings.cue: Listen to the ending: the noun ends '-gət'; the verb ends '-gate'.

origin: Latin 'delegare', to send away or entrust.

upgrade.plain: You should give some of your tasks to the new team members.
upgrade.model: You should delegate some of your tasks.

definition: Open and honest, with nothing hidden.

examples.text: The marking criteria should be transparent so everyone knows what's expected.
We want to be transparent with parents about how sets are decided.
Let's be transparent with the client about the delay and why it happened.
The letting agent wasn't transparent about the fees.

otherMeanings.meaning: Literally: clear enough to see through.
otherMeanings.example: Liquids go in a transparent bag at security.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of an excuse or lie: easy to see through; obvious.
otherMeanings.example: His excuse was transparent: everyone knew he had overslept.
otherMeanings.cue: Praise for a process, but criticism for an excuse or a motive.

origin: Latin 'trans', through, and 'parere', to appear: you can see through it.

upgrade.plain: We should be honest and open about the costs.
upgrade.model: We should be transparent about the costs.

definition: Significantly difficult or important; not simple.

examples.text: Getting ethics approval in time is a non-trivial challenge.
Proving it for all n is non-trivial; that's why it's a stretch question.
Migrating the auth system is non-trivial; let's estimate it properly.
Getting four families to agree on a restaurant is non-trivial.

otherMeanings.meaning: In maths, a non-trivial solution is one that isn't the obvious (usually zero) one.
otherMeanings.example: Show that the equation has a non-trivial solution.

commonMistake: Often an understatement in tech and maths circles; to outsiders it may sound like jargon.
origin: From maths: a 'trivial' solution is the obvious one, e.g. x = 0.

upgrade.plain: This change will take quite a lot of work.
upgrade.model: This change is non-trivial.

definition: A quick check to make sure something is reasonable and has no obvious errors.

examples.text: Could you give my introduction a quick sanity check before I submit?
Do a sanity check: could a person really be 15 metres tall?
Can I get a sanity check on this query before I run it on production?
Can you sanity-check this recipe? Two tablespoons of salt seems a lot.

synonyms.note: Reminder of the true situation; often about expectations.

origin: From checking that a result is 'sane', or sensible.

upgrade.plain: Can you quickly look at this to check it makes sense?
upgrade.model: Can you give this a quick sanity check?

definition: To accept full responsibility for a task, problem or outcome.

examples.text: I'll take ownership of the referencing so it's consistent throughout.
I want pupils to take ownership of their learning, not wait to be told.
Who's taking ownership of the follow-up actions from the incident?
I'll take ownership of the barbecue this year.

origin: From 'own', to possess: treating the task as your own.

upgrade.plain: I'll be responsible for fixing this.
upgrade.model: I'll take ownership of fixing this.

definition: An advance warning or piece of information so someone can prepare.

examples.text: Just a heads-up: the seminar has moved to room 2.14.
Thanks for the heads-up about the fire drill.
Heads-up: I'm deploying a database migration at 3 p.m.
Thanks for the heads-up about the roadworks.

origin: From the call to look up (lift your head) and watch out.

upgrade.plain: I'm telling you now so you're ready: the meeting has moved.
upgrade.model: Just a heads-up: the meeting has moved.

definition: To make brief contact with someone to catch up or check progress.

examples.text: Let's touch base on Thursday to see how the survey is going.
I'll touch base with his form tutor before parents' evening.
Can we touch base after lunch about the release plan?
Let's touch base on Sunday about Mum's birthday.

synonyms.note: Brief contact to see how things are.

commonMistake: Some find it corporate jargon; in casual British speech 'catch up' or 'have a quick chat' sounds warmer.
origin: From baseball, where a runner must touch each base.

upgrade.plain: I'll contact you next week to see how it's going.
upgrade.model: I'll touch base with you next week.

definition: A situation where you have to learn a lot very quickly.

examples.text: The first term of university was a steep learning curve.
Teaching A-level physics for the first time has been a steep learning curve.
Rust has a steep learning curve, but it pays off.
Becoming a parent was a steep learning curve.

synonyms.term: thrown in at the deep end
synonyms.note: Expected to cope with something difficult with no preparation.

commonMistake: Technically a steep curve means fast learning, but in everyday use it means 'hard to learn', and that's how everyone understands it.
origin: From psychology graphs plotting learning against time or attempts.

upgrade.plain: I had to learn a lot very quickly in my new job.
upgrade.model: My new job was a steep learning curve.

definition: To resolve small problems or difficulties.

examples.text: We still need to iron out who's presenting which section.
There are a few issues with the timetable to iron out before September.
We've ironed out most of the bugs in the beta.
We still need to iron out who's hosting Christmas.

synonyms.note: Make a problem seem less serious, often in relationships.

origin: From ironing creases out of clothes.

upgrade.plain: We need to fix a few small problems before launch.
upgrade.model: We need to iron out a few problems before launch.

definition: It's your turn to make a decision or take action.

examples.text: I've sent the draft to my supervisor, so the ball's in her court.
I've offered three meeting times; the ball's in the parents' court now.
We've answered their questions, so the ball's in the client's court.
I've said sorry, so the ball's in her court now.

collocations: the ball is in your court
put the ball in their court
origin: From tennis: the ball is on your side, so you have to play it.

upgrade.plain: I've done my part; now you need to decide.
upgrade.model: I've done my part; the ball's in your court.

definition: To start an activity or process.

examples.text: I'll get the ball rolling by sharing my notes on the first reading.
To get the ball rolling, tell your partner one thing you remember from last lesson.
Let's get the ball rolling on the hiring process this week.
I'll get the ball rolling on the holiday by looking at some cottages.

origin: Probably from ball games that begin when the ball is put into play.

upgrade.plain: I'll start the discussion with a question.
upgrade.model: I'll get the ball rolling with a question.

definition: Having the same understanding or agreeing about something.

examples.text: Let's make sure we're on the same page about the word limit.
It helps when home and school are on the same page about phones.
Before we estimate, let's check we're all on the same page about the scope.
Let's make sure we're on the same page about the wedding budget.

collocations: get everyone on the same page
make sure we're on the same page

synonyms.term: singing from the same hymn sheet
synonyms.note: Very British; presenting a united message.

origin: From everyone reading from the same page in a book or script.

upgrade.plain: I want to check we all understand the plan the same way.
upgrade.model: I want to check we're all on the same page.

definition: A situation that is unclear, without clear rules or a clear right answer.

examples.text: Using AI to check grammar is a grey area in the academic integrity policy.
Whether hoodies count as uniform is a bit of a grey area.
Who owns the shared component is a grey area; let's clarify it.
Whether the dog counts as a wedding guest is a grey area.

collocations: a bit of a grey area

synonyms.note: Unclear and possibly a bit dishonest.

commonMistake: British spelling: 'grey'; 'gray' is American.
origin: Neither black nor white: between clear right and wrong.

upgrade.plain: The rules aren't clear about this situation.
upgrade.model: This is a grey area in the rules.

definition: To make yourself do something difficult or unpleasant that you've been avoiding.

examples.text: I finally bit the bullet and rewrote the whole methodology chapter.
We need to bite the bullet and call the parents about this.
Let's bite the bullet and upgrade the framework; we can't keep patching.
I finally bit the bullet and booked the dentist.

synonyms.note: Very British: deal with a problem boldly.
Accept the consequences of your actions.

origin: Popularly said to come from patients biting a bullet during surgery without anaesthetic.

upgrade.plain: I'll just do the hard thing and tell them.
upgrade.model: I'll bite the bullet and tell them.

definition: To do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often reducing quality.

examples.text: Don't cut corners on the referencing; markers notice.
We can't cut corners on safety in the practical.
We cut corners on tests to hit the deadline and paid for it later.
Don't cut corners when you hire a builder.

origin: From taking the shortest route by going across a corner instead of around it.

upgrade.plain: We shouldn't do a rushed, cheap job on security.
upgrade.model: We shouldn't cut corners on security.

definition: To make more effort than is expected.

examples.text: She went the extra mile and interviewed the author for her project.
Thank you for going the extra mile with the revision sessions.
Support went the extra mile to get that customer back online.
The hotel staff went the extra mile for my mum's birthday.

collocations: willing to go the extra mile

synonyms.note: 'Went above and beyond': common in praise.

origin: From the Sermon on the Mount: 'whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two'.

upgrade.plain: He always does more than he needs to for customers.
upgrade.model: He always goes the extra mile for customers.

definition: Used when a plan has failed and you must start again.

examples.text: The ethics committee rejected our design, so it's back to the drawing board.
That seating plan didn't work at all; back to the drawing board.
The prototype failed the load test, so it's back to the drawing board.
The cottage is fully booked, so it's back to the drawing board.

collocations: it's back to the drawing board
go back to the drawing board

synonyms.note: Plainer; may keep parts of the plan.

origin: From engineers and architects returning to their drawing boards to redesign.

upgrade.plain: The idea didn't work, so we have to start again.
upgrade.model: The idea didn't work, so it's back to the drawing board.

definition: To start something new and immediately work effectively.

examples.text: Doing the summer reading means you'll hit the ground running in September.
If the resources are ready, we can hit the ground running on day one.
Good onboarding docs help new joiners hit the ground running.
We hit the ground running on holiday and saw five sights on day one.

collocations: ready to hit the ground running

synonyms.term: get off to a flying start

origin: Possibly military: soldiers landing from aircraft and moving straight away.

upgrade.plain: I want to be productive straight away when I start.
upgrade.model: I want to hit the ground running when I start.

definition: An obvious problem that everyone is aware of but nobody wants to mention.

examples.text: The elephant in the room is that two people in the group haven't contributed.
The elephant in the room is that we don't have enough staff for this.
Can we address the elephant in the room? We're three weeks behind.
At family dinners, Uncle Pete's new car is the elephant in the room.

collocations: address the elephant in the room
the elephant in the room is

synonyms.note: Something supposedly secret that everyone knows.

origin: Something so large it's impossible to miss, yet everyone pretends not to see it.

upgrade.plain: Let's talk about the obvious problem nobody is mentioning: the budget.
upgrade.model: Let's address the elephant in the room: the budget.

definition: To stop working on something, for now or for good.

examples.text: We've been in the library for six hours; let's call it a day.
After 30 years in teaching, he's decided to call it a day.
It's 7 p.m.; let's call it a day and look at the bug fresh tomorrow.
We've been walking for six hours; let's call it a day.

collocations: decide to call it a day

synonyms.note: Finish, often a meeting or event.
Informal British: finish work for the day.
British: bring something to an end, like last orders in a pub.

origin: Originally 'call it half a day', from at least the 19th century.

upgrade.plain: We've done enough for today; let's stop.
upgrade.model: We've done enough; let's call it a day.

definition: Feeling slightly ill.

examples.text: I'm a bit under the weather, so I'll join the seminar online.
Half the class are under the weather this week, so we'll recap on Monday.
I'm feeling under the weather; I'll work from home today.
I'm a bit under the weather, so I'll skip the party.

origin: Possibly nautical: seasick passengers went below deck, away from the weather.

upgrade.plain: I'm feeling a little ill today.
upgrade.model: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.

definition: Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good.

examples.text: Failing my driving test was a blessing in disguise; I had more time to revise.
The cancelled trip was a blessing in disguise: we caught up on coursework.
The outage was a blessing in disguise; it exposed gaps in our monitoring.
Missing the train was a blessing in disguise; we found a lovely café.

collocations: turn out to be a blessing in disguise

synonyms.term: every cloud has a silver lining
synonyms.note: Proverb: something good comes from bad.
Something good that happened by chance.

origin: From an 18th-century hymn by James Hervey.

upgrade.plain: Losing that contract was bad at first but actually good for us.
upgrade.model: Losing that contract was a blessing in disguise.

definition: To decide what to do as a situation develops, rather than planning in advance.

examples.text: I don't know if I'll make the social; I'll play it by ear.
If the weather's bad, we'll play it by ear and maybe move the lesson indoors.
We'll play it by ear and decide on the rollout after the first day's metrics.
We'll play it by ear and head to the beach if it's sunny.

collocations: we'll just play it by ear

synonyms.note: Informal; do it without preparation (more risky).

origin: From playing music by listening, without written notes.

upgrade.plain: We'll decide later depending on what happens.
upgrade.model: We'll play it by ear.

definition: To keep someone informed about something.

examples.text: Please keep me in the loop if the deadline changes.
I'll keep you in the loop about his progress this half-term.
Keep the support team in the loop about the release timeline.
Keep me in the loop about Gran's hospital appointment.

origin: From a communication loop: being part of the circle of people who get information.

upgrade.plain: Please tell me about any changes.
upgrade.model: Please keep me in the loop.

definition: To ask someone who knows a lot about a subject for advice or information.

examples.text: Could I pick your brains about applying for a master's?
I picked the head of science's brains about teaching electricity.
Can I pick your brains about caching strategies over coffee?
Can I pick your brains about buying a second-hand car?

commonMistake: British English usually says 'brains' (plural); American English often says 'brain'.
origin: From picking food off a bone: taking what's useful from someone's mind.

upgrade.plain: Can I ask you for some advice about the job market?
upgrade.model: Can I pick your brains about the job market?

definition: To start dealing with something that will cause many more problems.

examples.text: Questioning the grading would open a can of worms for the whole cohort.
Changing the uniform policy mid-year would open a can of worms.
Touching the billing code opens a can of worms; it affects every product.
Asking about the will would open a can of worms.

synonyms.note: More dramatic; releases many unexpected troubles.

origin: From fishing bait: once opened, worms wriggle everywhere and are hard to contain.

upgrade.plain: If we ask about that, it'll cause lots of other problems.
upgrade.model: If we ask about that, we'll open a can of worms.

definition: A polite request for someone to be patient while you do something.

examples.text: Bear with me; I'm just finding the right slide.
Bear with me while I get the projector working.
Bear with me, I'll share my screen in a second.
Bear with me; I'm just finding my reading glasses.

commonMistake: It's 'bear with me' (be patient), not 'bare with me' (which would mean undressing together!).
origin: 'Bear' in the old sense of tolerate or endure, as in 'I can't bear it'.

upgrade.plain: Wait a moment while I find the file.
upgrade.model: Bear with me while I find the file.

definition: To think of an idea, plan or solution.

examples.text: We need to come up with a research question by Friday.
Can your group come up with three ways to speed up the reaction?
She came up with an elegant fix for the caching issue.
We need to come up with a name for the new puppy.

synonyms.note: Formal; form an idea in the mind.

origin: From 'come up', to arise or appear.

upgrade.plain: We need to think of a better name.
upgrade.model: We need to come up with a better name.

definition: To suggest an idea or plan for others to consider.

examples.text: In this essay, I put forward three reasons for the decline.
I've put forward a proposal for a maths club on Wednesdays.
Several options were put forward, but we chose the simplest.
My aunt put forward a plan for Christmas that suits everyone.

synonyms.note: British: present for discussion; American: postpone!

otherMeanings.meaning: To move an event to an earlier time, or a clock to a later one.
otherMeanings.example: The meeting's been put forward to Monday, and the clocks go forward on Sunday.
otherMeanings.cue: Clocks: 'spring forward, fall back'. In late March, British clocks go forward an hour.

otherMeanings.meaning: To nominate someone.
otherMeanings.example: She was put forward for the teaching award.

origin: Literally placing something in front of people.

upgrade.plain: I'd like to suggest a new plan.
upgrade.model: I'd like to put forward a new plan.

definition: To take further action on something, or check its progress.

examples.text: I'm following up on my email about the extension request.
I'll follow up on the missing homework with a call home.
Can you follow up on the security review? It's been a week.
I'm following up on my complaint about the missing parcel.

synonyms.note: British, informal: remind someone to act.

commonMistake: Verb: 'follow up' (two words). Noun/adjective: 'follow-up' (a follow-up email).
origin: From following a trail further to its end.

upgrade.plain: I'm writing again about my message from last week.
upgrade.model: I'm following up on my message from last week.

definition: To tell someone about an idea to get their opinion or approval.

examples.text: Can I run my essay plan by you before I start writing?
I'll run the trip idea by the head before we tell the children.
Let me run this approach by the architect before I build it.
Let me run the holiday dates by my partner first.

origin: From passing something quickly in front of someone to look at.

upgrade.plain: I'll ask my manager what she thinks of the idea.
upgrade.model: I'll run the idea by my manager.

definition: To improve a skill or knowledge you used to have but have partly forgotten.

examples.text: I need to brush up on my statistics before the research methods module.
I brushed up on my chemistry before covering the Year 11 class.
I'm brushing up on SQL before the data engineering interview.
I'm brushing up on my French before our trip to Paris.

synonyms.note: British: study again for an exam.

origin: From brushing dust off something you haven't used for a while.

upgrade.plain: I should practise my Spanish again before the trip.
upgrade.model: I should brush up on my Spanish before the trip.

definition: To start to understand and deal with something difficult.

examples.text: I'm still getting to grips with referencing in Harvard style.
Year 9 are getting to grips with simultaneous equations.
It took me a month to get to grips with the codebase.
Dad is still getting to grips with his new phone.

synonyms.note: Informal; learn how to do something.

origin: From wrestling: taking hold of your opponent.

upgrade.plain: I'm slowly learning how the new system works.
upgrade.model: I'm slowly getting to grips with the new system.

definition: To consider the advantages and disadvantages of something before deciding.

examples.text: I'm weighing up whether to do a placement year.
Weigh up the evidence on both sides before writing your conclusion.
We need to weigh up the cost of building it ourselves against buying a licence.
We're weighing up whether to get a dog.

collocations: weigh up the pros and cons
origin: From weighing goods on scales: which side is heavier?

upgrade.plain: I'm thinking about the good and bad points of each job offer.
upgrade.model: I'm weighing up both job offers.

definition: To add more detail to a plan, idea or piece of writing.

examples.text: Flesh out your second paragraph with an example from the text.
We'll flesh out the scheme of work in the next department meeting.
Can you flesh out the ticket with acceptance criteria?
Let's flesh out the plans for the barbecue.

origin: From adding flesh to a skeleton.

upgrade.plain: Could you add more details to the proposal?
upgrade.model: Could you flesh out the proposal?

definition: To decide that something is not possible or not suitable.

examples.text: We've ruled out an online survey because of the low response rate.
Before deciding it's a reaction, we need to rule out human error.
We've ruled out the network; the issue is in the application.
We've ruled out camping; it's going to pour.

origin: From drawing a line through something with a ruler.

upgrade.plain: We can't say for sure it won't happen.
upgrade.model: We can't rule it out.

definition: To appear or happen unexpectedly.

examples.text: Something's cropped up, so I can't make the group meeting.
This question type crops up every year in the exam.
The same bug keeps cropping up in different parts of the app.
Something's cropped up, so I can't make the cinema tonight.

origin: Probably from mining: rock that 'crops out' at the surface.

upgrade.plain: Something unexpected has happened, so I need to leave early.
upgrade.model: Something's cropped up, so I need to leave early.

definition: To contribute money or help; also, to add a comment to a conversation.

examples.text: We all chipped in for our supervisor's leaving present.
Feel free to chip in if you have a different method.
Do chip in if I've missed anything from the incident timeline.
Everyone chipped in for Sarah's leaving present.

origin: From poker: putting chips into the pot.

upgrade.plain: Please add your thoughts if you have any.
upgrade.model: Please chip in if you have any thoughts.

definition: To understand and accept an idea or suggestion, and act on it.

examples.text: I've taken your feedback on board and restructured the essay.
Thanks; we'll take that on board when we review the homework policy.
We've taken the users' comments on board in the redesign.
I've taken your advice on board and booked a proper holiday.

commonMistake: Very common in British English and polite, but used too often it can sound like you're dismissing a point. Follow it with what you'll actually do.
origin: Nautical: loading cargo onto a ship.

upgrade.plain: I've listened to your comments and will use them.
upgrade.model: I've taken your comments on board.

definition: A task or request that is very difficult to achieve.

examples.text: Writing 10,000 words in two weeks is a tall order.
Covering the whole topic in one lesson is a tall order.
Rebuilding the app by Christmas is a tall order, but let's see what's possible.
Getting the kids to bed by seven is a tall order.

collocations: a bit of a tall order
origin: 'Tall' in old American slang meant excessive or exaggerated.

upgrade.plain: Finishing it by Friday will be very difficult.
upgrade.model: Finishing it by Friday is a tall order.

definition: To avoid talking about the main point, especially because it is awkward.

examples.text: I won't beat about the bush: your draft needs major changes.
Let's not beat about the bush: his behaviour has to change.
I'll not beat about the bush; the project is over budget.
Don't beat about the bush: did you scratch my car?

synonyms.note: Formal: avoid giving a direct answer.

commonMistake: British English says 'beat about the bush'; American English usually says 'beat around the bush'.
origin: From hunting: beaters hit bushes to drive birds out, rather than catching them directly.

upgrade.plain: I'll be direct: we can't afford it.
upgrade.model: I won't beat about the bush: we can't afford it.

term: get the wrong end of the stick
ipa: /ɡet ðə ˌrɒŋ ˌend əv ðə ˈstɪk/
definition: To misunderstand something completely.

examples.text: I think I got the wrong end of the stick; I thought the essay was due today.
Some parents got the wrong end of the stick about the new setting policy.
Sorry, I got the wrong end of the stick; you meant the staging server, not production.
Our neighbour got the wrong end of the stick and thought we were moving.

collocations: get hold of the wrong end of the stick
got the wrong end of the stick
origin: Typically British; the exact origin is uncertain.
forms: got the wrong end of the stick
getting the wrong end of the stick

upgrade.plain: Sorry, I completely misunderstood what you meant.
upgrade.model: Sorry, I got the wrong end of the stick.

definition: Not something I like or enjoy; a polite way to express a dislike.

examples.text: Group presentations aren't really my cup of tea, but I'll give it a go.
Musicals aren't my cup of tea, but the school show was brilliant.
Front-end work isn't my cup of tea; I prefer the back end.
Karaoke isn't really my cup of tea.

collocations: not really my cup of tea
just not my cup of tea
origin: British: from the 1900s, when 'my cup of tea' meant something you liked.

upgrade.plain: I don't really like horror films.
upgrade.model: Horror films aren't really my cup of tea.

definition: Exactly right or accurate (British, informal).

examples.text: Your summary of the argument is spot on.
Spot on! That's exactly the right unit.
Your estimate was spot on: it took exactly three days.
Your directions to the pub were spot on.

origin: From hitting the exact spot on a target.

upgrade.plain: Your answer is exactly right.
upgrade.model: Your answer is spot on.

definition: To unfairly change the rules or targets after something has started.

examples.text: The department moved the goalposts by changing the word limit a week before the deadline.
The exam board keeps moving the goalposts on coursework requirements.
We agreed on the requirements in January; they can't keep moving the goalposts.
My landlord keeps moving the goalposts on the deposit.

synonyms.note: In projects: the requirements gradually grow.

origin: From football: moving the goal makes scoring unfairly harder.

upgrade.plain: It's unfair that they keep changing what they want.
upgrade.model: They keep moving the goalposts.

definition: Postponed or given low priority for now.

examples.text: I've put the society website on the back burner until exams are over.
The new reading scheme is on the back burner until next year.
Let's put the redesign on the back burner and focus on performance.
The loft conversion is on the back burner until next year.

collocations: put something on the back burner
on the back burner for now

synonyms.note: British business: set aside to discuss later.

origin: From cooking: pans on the back of the stove simmer while you focus on the front.

upgrade.plain: We'll postpone this project for a few months.
upgrade.model: We'll put this project on the back burner for a few months.

definition: Very pleased (British, informal).

examples.text: I'm chuffed to bits with my dissertation mark.
The Year 9s were chuffed when their bridge held two kilos.
The client was chuffed with the demo.
Mum was chuffed with her birthday flowers.

commonMistake: Great with colleagues you know, but too casual for a formal report.
origin: From the dialect word 'chuff', meaning puffed up or plump.

upgrade.plain: I'm really pleased with how it went.
upgrade.model: I'm chuffed with how it went.

definition: Extremely tired; also, of a thing, broken or worn out.

examples.text: I'm knackered after three exams in a row.
By the last week of term, every teacher is knackered.
I'm knackered; the release went on until midnight.
I'm knackered after moving house all weekend.

synonyms.note: British informal; very close in meaning.

commonMistake: Very informal: fine with friends and close colleagues, but avoid it with parents or clients.
origin: Possibly from 'knacker', a person who bought worn-out horses.

upgrade.plain: I'm really tired after today.
upgrade.model: I'm knackered after today.

definition: Bitterly disappointed (British, informal).

examples.text: I was gutted to miss a first by two marks.
The team were gutted to lose the quiz final.
We're gutted the feature didn't make the release.
We were gutted when the match was rained off.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of a building: with its insides destroyed or removed.
otherMeanings.example: The old pub was gutted by fire last year.
otherMeanings.cue: About a building (or a fish) it's literal.

commonMistake: 'I'm gutted for you' is a warm way to show sympathy.
origin: From gutting a fish: as if your insides had been taken out.

upgrade.plain: I was very disappointed not to get the job.
upgrade.model: I was gutted not to get the job.

definition: Unnecessary fuss or hassle; as a verb ('faff about'), to waste time doing things inefficiently.

examples.text: Formatting references by hand is such a faff.
Getting thirty laptops logged in is always a faff.
Let's stop faffing about with the config and use the defaults.
Getting the kids out of the door is always a faff.

synonyms.note: British, slightly old-fashioned; a lot of fuss.

origin: From an old dialect word for a puff of wind: lots of bluster, little result.

upgrade.plain: Setting up the printer is really annoying and takes ages.
upgrade.model: Setting up the printer is a real faff.

definition: Having little or no money (informal).

examples.text: I'm skint until my student loan comes in.
Plenty of families are skint at the end of the month, so let's keep the trip cheap.
The start-up was skint, so we hosted everything on the free tier.
I'm skint until payday, so no takeaway this week.

synonyms.note: Common in both British and American English.

commonMistake: Fine about yourself, but avoid describing other people as 'skint' in formal settings.
origin: A variant of 'skinned': as if stripped bare.

upgrade.plain: I don't have any money until payday.
upgrade.model: I'm skint until payday.

definition: Slightly hungry.

examples.text: I'm a bit peckish; shall we grab a snack before the lecture?
Pupils get peckish by period 4, so I keep that lesson lively.
Anyone peckish? I'm ordering pastries for the workshop.
I'm a bit peckish; is there any cake left?

origin: From 'peck', like a bird pecking at food.

upgrade.plain: I'm a little hungry.
upgrade.model: I'm feeling a bit peckish.

definition: Arranged, fixed or dealt with (informal).

examples.text: The group presentation is sorted; we've each got a section.
Cover for my Year 10 class is sorted.
The login bug is sorted and deployed.
The train tickets are sorted, so we just need to pack.

otherMeanings.meaning: Of a person: well organised and emotionally settled.
otherMeanings.example: She's really sorted: mortgage, pension, the lot.

otherMeanings.meaning: 'Sorted?' as a question: is everything OK? Have you got what you need?
otherMeanings.example: 'Sorted for tickets?' 'Yep, all sorted.'

origin: From 'sort out', to put in order.

upgrade.plain: Don't worry, I've dealt with the booking.
upgrade.model: Don't worry, the booking's sorted.

definition: Slightly rude or bold in a playful way; in British slang, also a small treat ('a cheeky biscuit').

examples.text: Fancy a cheeky coffee before the seminar?
He gave a cheeky answer, but it was actually correct.
Can I ask a cheeky favour? Could you review my PR today?
Shall we have a cheeky pint after work?

commonMistake: 'A cheeky favour' politely admits you're asking a lot.
origin: From 'cheek', meaning insolent talk, since the 1800s.

upgrade.plain: Could I ask you for a favour, even though it's a bit much?
upgrade.model: Could I ask a cheeky favour?

definition: A cup of tea (sometimes coffee).

examples.text: Let's have a cuppa and plan the essay.
I'll mark these with a cuppa at break.
Shall we grab a cuppa and talk it through?
Pop the kettle on and we'll have a cuppa.

collocations: put the kettle on for a cuppa
origin: How 'cup of (tea)' sounds in quick speech.

upgrade.plain: Would you like a cup of tea?
upgrade.model: Fancy a cuppa?

definition: Something very easy to do.

examples.text: After all that revision, the exam was a doddle.
Once you know the trick, these equations are a doddle.
Adding the new field was a doddle thanks to the migrations tool.
Putting up the shelves was a doddle.

synonyms.note: So easy a child could do it.

origin: Possibly from 'doddle', to toddle along: an easy stroll.

upgrade.plain: The test was really easy.
upgrade.model: The test was a doddle.

definition: And there you are: said after simple instructions to show how easy something is.

examples.text: Upload the file, click submit, and Bob's your uncle.
Multiply both sides by three and Bob's your uncle.
Run the script, restart the server, and Bob's your uncle.
Add the milk, give it a stir, and Bob's your uncle.

origin: Uncertain. One popular story links it to a Victorian prime minister who promoted his nephew.

upgrade.plain: Plug it in, press the button, and it's done.
upgrade.model: Plug it in, press the button, and Bob's your uncle.

definition: To tease or make fun of someone; also, to be unreasonable ('Are you taking the mickey?').

examples.text: Are you taking the mickey, or do you really like my poster?

Ignore him; he's just taking the mickey about my commit messages.
My brothers always take the mickey out of my driving.

synonyms.note: British: annoy someone as a joke.

commonMistake: 'Are you taking the mickey?' can also mean 'Are you being unreasonable?', e.g. about a price.
origin: Possibly Cockney rhyming slang; the exact origin is uncertain.

upgrade.plain: Are you joking? That price is ridiculous.
upgrade.model: Are you taking the mickey? That price is ridiculous.

definition: Utterly astonished.

examples.text: I was gobsmacked when I saw my grade.
The class were gobsmacked when the balloon stuck to the wall.
We were gobsmacked by how many people signed up on day one.
I was gobsmacked by the price of a sandwich at the airport.

synonyms.note: Shocked into silence; can be negative.

origin: 'Gob' is British slang for mouth: like clapping a hand over your mouth in shock.

upgrade.plain: I was really surprised by the result.
upgrade.model: I was gobsmacked by the result.

definition: A period of two weeks.

examples.text: The essay is due in a fortnight.
We'll have a test on this in a fortnight.
Our sprints last a fortnight.
We're off to Cornwall for a fortnight in August.

synonyms.note: Ambiguous: can mean twice a week or every two weeks.

commonMistake: Many Americans don't use 'fortnight', so say 'two weeks' with international colleagues. 'Fortnightly' avoids the ambiguity of 'biweekly'.
origin: Old English 'fēowertīene niht': fourteen nights.

upgrade.plain: We meet every two weeks.
upgrade.model: We meet every fortnight.

definition: To go wrong.

examples.text: Our group project went pear-shaped when two people dropped out.
The practical went pear-shaped when the Bunsen burners wouldn't light.
The deployment went pear-shaped at the last minute.
The barbecue went pear-shaped when it started to pour.

origin: Possibly RAF slang from the 1940s: a badly flown loop ends up pear-shaped rather than round.

upgrade.plain: Everything went wrong at the end.
upgrade.model: Everything went pear-shaped at the end.

definition: To have a long, relaxed chat.

examples.text: We had a natter about the reading instead of revising.
Parents' evening overran because one dad wanted a natter.
Let's have a natter over coffee rather than another meeting.
I popped round for a natter with my neighbour.

origin: From the dialect word 'gnatter', to grumble or chatter.

upgrade.plain: Let's have a relaxed chat at lunch.
upgrade.model: Let's have a natter at lunch.

definition: Used to accept a point as reasonable, even if you don't fully agree.

examples.text: You'd rather present first? Fair enough.
Fair enough, that's a valid method too.
Fair enough; let's go with your approach and review it next sprint.
You'd rather stay in tonight? Fair enough.

otherMeanings.meaning: A polite way to drop a subject, even though you don't agree.
otherMeanings.example: 'I'd rather not talk about it.' 'Fair enough.'

origin: A plain combination: 'fair' (just) plus 'enough'.

upgrade.plain: OK, I accept that's a reasonable point.
upgrade.model: Fair enough, that's a reasonable point.

definition: Thanks (informal); also goodbye, or a toast when drinking.

examples.text: Cheers for lending me your notes.
Cheers, that's really helpful.
Cheers for the quick review!
Cheers for picking me up from the station.

commonMistake: Fine with colleagues you know, but use 'Thank you' or 'Many thanks' in formal emails.
origin: From 'cheer', which once meant face or mood, and later a shout of encouragement.

upgrade.plain: Thanks for your help.
upgrade.model: Cheers for your help.

definition: Quite good, often better than expected (classic British understatement).

examples.text: A 68 on my first essay: not too shabby.
Not too shabby! Nearly everyone got question 5 right.
Load time down to 300 milliseconds. Not too shabby.
A sunny weekend in Manchester? Not too shabby.

collocations: not too shabby for a first attempt

synonyms.note: In British speech, often means genuinely good.

origin: 'Shabby' means worn or poor quality; denying it is typical British understatement.

upgrade.plain: That's pretty good for a first try.
upgrade.model: That's not too shabby for a first try.

definition: Fairly or moderately: in British English, 'quite good' usually means 'decent, but not great'.

examples.text: My essay mark was quite good, but my tutor said the argument needed more depth.
Their predictions were quite good, though nobody spotted the anomalous result.
The new build is quite good, but it's still slower than we'd like.
The film was quite good; I wouldn't rush to see it again.

synonyms.note: Milder and flatter: 'fairly good' is never high praise.

otherMeanings.meaning: Completely or totally, with words that cannot be graded.
otherMeanings.example: You're quite right; I hadn't thought of that.
otherMeanings.cue: With 'right', 'sure', 'certain', 'different' or 'impossible', 'quite' means 'completely'.

otherMeanings.meaning: Surprisingly good, when said with enthusiasm.
otherMeanings.example: Actually, that's quite good! I didn't expect to like it.

otherMeanings.meaning: 'Quite!' on its own: I completely agree.

origin: Middle English, from 'quit' in the sense 'free, clear': it first meant 'completely'.

definition: Not willing to make the effort.

examples.text: I can't be bothered to cook, so it's beans on toast again.

I can't be bothered to cook tonight; let's get fish and chips.

commonMistake: Said about others it can sound critical; say it about yourself, with a smile.
origin: From 'bother', to take trouble over something.

upgrade.plain: I don't feel like going out tonight.
upgrade.model: I can't be bothered to go out tonight.

examples.text: Library or café? I'm easy.
Tuesday or Thursday for the department meeting? I'm easy.
Tabs or spaces? Honestly, I'm easy, as long as we're consistent.
Pizza or curry? I'm easy.

synonyms.note: Polite, puts the other person first.

origin: From 'easy' in the sense of relaxed or untroubled.

upgrade.plain: I don't mind; you choose where we go.
upgrade.model: I'm easy; you choose where we go.

definition: To visit or go somewhere briefly (also 'pop out', 'pop round', 'pop over').

examples.text: I'll pop in to the library on my way home.
Do pop in after school if you'd like to talk about his progress.

I'll pop in to see Gran on the way home.

origin: From 'pop', a quick, sudden movement.

upgrade.plain: I'll visit you briefly after lunch.
upgrade.model: I'll pop in after lunch.

definition: Of very poor quality, or bad at something (informal British). As a noun: waste, or nonsense.

examples.text: I'm rubbish at statistics, so I'm going to the drop-in sessions.
Don't say you're rubbish at maths; say you haven't learnt it yet.
The first version was rubbish, but it taught us what users wanted.
The weather's been rubbish all week.

otherMeanings.meaning: (verb) To criticise something harshly, or dismiss it as worthless.
otherMeanings.example: Critics rubbished the plan as unworkable.

otherMeanings.meaning: 'Rubbish!' on its own: nonsense!
otherMeanings.example: 'You're too old to learn the guitar.' 'Rubbish!'

commonMistake: British 'rubbish' (and 'bin') where American English says 'trash' or 'garbage'.
origin: From Old French 'robeux', broken stone and rubble.

upgrade.plain: I'm really bad at remembering names.
upgrade.model: I'm rubbish at remembering names.

definition: A difficult or annoying situation (British understatement).

examples.text: Finding a quiet study space during exams is a bit of a nightmare.
Parking at school is a bit of a nightmare on parents' evening.
Merging those two branches was a bit of a nightmare.
Parking in town on a Saturday is a bit of a nightmare.

origin: The softening 'a bit of' is pure British understatement: it's usually a full nightmare.

upgrade.plain: Travelling during the strike was really difficult.
upgrade.model: Travelling during the strike was a bit of a nightmare.

examples.text: A 5,000-word essay by Monday? You're having a laugh.
Mark 120 books by tomorrow? They're having a laugh.

Twelve quid for a sandwich? You're having a laugh.

otherMeanings.cue: 'You're having a laugh' is disbelief; 'we were having a laugh' is fun.

commonMistake: Note the British long 'a' in 'laugh': /lɑːf/.
origin: From 'have a laugh', to joke around.

upgrade.plain: They want it finished by tonight? That can't be serious.
upgrade.model: They want it finished by tonight? They're having a laugh.

definition: It's not difficult to understand or do.

examples.text: Referencing isn't rocket science, but it is fiddly.

Changing a fuse isn't rocket science.

commonMistake: Can sound dismissive if someone is struggling. Use it about tasks, not people.
origin: From the late 20th century, when rocket science stood for the hardest work imaginable.

upgrade.plain: It's simple; anyone can learn it.
upgrade.model: It's not rocket science; anyone can learn it.

term: throw a spanner in the works
definition: To cause a problem that stops a plan working.

examples.text: The library closing early threw a spanner in the works.
The surprise fire drill threw a spanner in the works.
The vendor's API change has thrown a spanner in the works.
The train strike threw a spanner in the works.

collocations: throw a spanner in the works

commonMistake: British English says 'spanner'; American English says 'throw a (monkey) wrench in the works'.
origin: From machinery: a spanner dropped into the gears jams everything.

upgrade.plain: The rain caused a problem for our plans.

definition: To manage somehow, despite lacking skill, knowledge or a plan.

examples.text: I didn't understand the reading, but I muddled through the seminar.
We muddled through the lesson without the projector.
We muddled through the outage with very little documentation.
We muddled through the flat-pack instructions in the end.

origin: Often called a very British ideal: getting there in the end without fuss or a plan.

upgrade.plain: We didn't have a plan, but we managed somehow.
upgrade.model: We didn't have a plan, but we muddled through.

definition: A polite phrase used just before disagreeing, often firmly.

examples.text: With all due respect, I think the data says something different.
With all due respect, the new timetable doesn't give pupils enough practice time.
With all due respect, that estimate doesn't include testing.
With all due respect, Dad, the satnav does know the way.

commonMistake: Despite the polite words, Britons hear it as 'I think you're wrong'. Use it sparingly.
origin: Originally formal courtesy; now a well-known signal of polite disagreement.

upgrade.plain: I disagree, but I don't want to be rude.
upgrade.model: With all due respect, I disagree.

definition: To want or like the idea of something (British, informal): 'Fancy a coffee?'

examples.text: Do you fancy revising together on Thursday?
Who fancies having a go at the board?
Fancy pairing on this bug after lunch?
Fancy a walk along the canal this afternoon?

otherMeanings.meaning: To find someone attractive.
otherMeanings.example: I think Sam fancies you: he laughs at all your jokes.
otherMeanings.cue: About a person rather than a thing, it's romantic: 'Do you fancy him?'

otherMeanings.meaning: (adjective) Elaborate, expensive or posh.
otherMeanings.example: We went somewhere fancy for her birthday.

otherMeanings.meaning: 'Fancy that!' or 'Fancy seeing you here!': an expression of surprise.
otherMeanings.example: Fancy seeing you here! I didn't know you lived round this way.

commonMistake: Using 'fancy' to mean 'want' is British; American English rarely uses it this way.
origin: Short for 'fantasy': to imagine having something.
